title.text: Pacific Economies & the Iran Oil Shock

subtitle.text: Assessing fuel dependency, energy vulnerability, and fiscal exposure across Pacific Island Countries and Territories

note.text: Pacific Island Countries and Territories (PICTs) are almost entirely dependent on imported petroleum fuels — for electricity generation, transport, fishing, and government operations. A spike in global diesel and petrol prices (e.g. triggered by conflict near the Strait of Hormuz) has an outsized impact on these small, isolated, import-dependent economies. The indicators below reveal the channels of vulnerability: fiscal strain, trade balance deterioration, high retail fuel costs, low renewable energy buffers, and expensive electricity for households and businesses.

subtitle.text: How much of each economy is consumed by fuel imports

note.text: A higher share means a larger macro hit when fuel prices rise. Countries above 10% of GDP face severe economic stress.
When fuel prices rise, countries with high fuel import shares face worsening trade deficits and currency pressure.

subtitle.text: The buffer against fossil fuel price shocks (2018)

note.text: Countries with near-zero renewable share are almost entirely diesel-dependent — the most exposed to a price shock.

subtitle.text: Baseline diesel cost before the shock

note.text: Countries already paying above USD 1.20/L are starting from a high base — even a 30–50% price spike would be devastating.
Already elevated retail prices mean households spend a high share of income on fuel and transport.

subtitle.text: Fiscal space available to absorb or subsidise a fuel price shock

note.text: Governments with thin revenue bases have little capacity to subsidise fuel, protect the poor, or invest in energy alternatives when a price shock hits.

**1. Electricity costs surge** — Most PICTs generate power from diesel. Higher diesel = higher power tariffs for households, businesses, hospitals, schools.

**2. Food prices rise** — Fishing (outboard motors), agriculture (irrigation pumps), and food transport all run on diesel.

**3. Trade deficits widen** — Fuel is 15–20% of imports for many PICTs. A price spike deepens deficits and drains foreign reserves.

**4. Government budgets strained** — Revenue-to-GDP is thin in most PICTs. Fuel subsidies or direct transfers are costly.

**5. Tourism disrupted** — Aviation fuel costs affect air travel prices, reducing arrivals to tourism-dependent economies like Fiji, Palau, and FSM.
